title: Indicator Removal: Network Share Connection Removal
shortTitle: Indicator Removal: Network Share Connection Removal
summary: Network Share Connection Removal is the deliberate disconnection of mapped drives and administrative share sessions that an intruder no longer needs. After using Server Message Block (SMB) shares to read files, drop tools, or reach another host, the attacker tears the connection down so that a later review of open sessions and stored credentials shows nothing unusual. The underlying actions are the same ones a help desk performs every day: the Windows net use command with the delete switch, net use with a wildcard to drop every mapping at once, or the equivalent umount and unmount verbs on Linux and macOS, plus removal of saved credentials and cleanup of the shared drive letters and registry entries that record them. Detection therefore leans on the lifetime of the connection rather than the disconnection itself. Authentication records on the target, such as Windows Security logon events of type 3 for network access and detailed share access events, still exist after the client forgets the mapping, and the real question is whether a session was briefly used for writes or service creation and then quietly removed by a process that is not a login script, a session manager, or a user logging off. Credential Manager entries and persisting drive letters that disappear, host pairs that connect repeatedly for short periods, and disconnection commands spawning from script interpreters rather than explorer are the strongest discriminators.

beginner.definition: Network share connection removal means an attacker closes a connection to a shared folder. Shared folders let computers read each other's files. Attackers use them to move tools and data. Then they disconnect so the trail looks smaller.
beginner.whyItMatters: Shared folders are one of the easiest ways to move through a network. When many computers connect to one server, that server keeps records. If an attacker removes their connection, the list of current connections looks clean. You then have to rely on history, not on what is open right now.
howItWorks: A shared folder lets computers on the same network read and write files in one place.
An attacker connects to that share using normal tools, or reuses an account they already stole.
Through the connection they copy tools, read documents, or run commands on the other computer.
When the work is done they disconnect, for example with the net use command and its delete option.
They may also remove saved credentials so no password remains in the credential store.
On Linux and macOS the same idea appears as a file system unmount instead of a Windows command.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel where guests sign a book in the lobby when they arrive. A thief signs in, takes what they need from a room, and then tears out their page from the book. The hotel manager sees no guest. Only the room record and the CCTV footage still prove a visit happened.
takeaways: Removing a share connection leaves a gap in the current list, not in the logs.
Windows keeps network logon records after the mapped drive is gone, so check those first.
Ask whether the disconnecting process is a person, a login script, or a script interpreter.

objectives: Describe how mapped drives and administrative shares allow file access across a network.
Explain why an attacker disconnects a share when it is no longer needed.
Identify the log and artifact types that record share use after disconnection.
Recognise normal drive mapping and unmapping activity in a business environment.
Outline how to correlate a short-lived share session with later suspicious activity.
